Six
siks
adj., n.
Old English siex; the cardinal one short of seven. In Scripture the number of man and his labor—made on the sixth day, set to work six days—and, tripled, the number of man in his rebellion.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Six is the number of man and of labor under the sun. Man was made on the sixth day, and to man the fourth commandment says, “six days you shall labor and do all your work,” before the seventh-day rest. Six is thus the working number, the number of the creature at his appointed task—good, God-given, but not the goal; it always looks toward the seventh, the Sabbath completion it cannot reach on its own. Because it falls one short of seven’s fullness, six can also signify man striving to be complete apart from God, and so becomes the number of rebellion when it is tripled. The mark of the beast is “the number of a man,” six hundred sixty-six—man exalting himself in a mock trinity, forever falling short of the seven of God. Rightly read, six humbles: it sets man in his creaturely place as a worker who must rest in God, not a god who never rests. The sixth-day creature is crowned only when he keeps the seventh-day Sabbath of his Maker.

Webster 1828 Definition

The number of man and his labor—created on the sixth day, set to six days’ work—and, tripled to 666, the number of man in proud rebellion, ever one short of the seven of God.

expand to see more

SIX, adj. One more than five; one less than seven. In Scripture the number of man, made on the sixth day, and of labor, the six working days that precede the Sabbath.

SIX, n. The creature’s number: good in its place, yet always short of seven’s completion. Tripled in Revelation’s 666, it marks man’s self-exaltation—“the number of a man”—a counterfeit fullness that never arrives at the rest of God.

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:9 — "Six days you shall labor and do all your work,"

Genesis 1:31 — "Then God saw everything that He had made, and indeed it was very good. So the evening and the morning were the sixth day."

Revelation 13:18 — "Here is wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast — for the number is that of a man, and his number is six hundred and sixty-six."

Genesis 1:14 — "Then God said, "Let there be lights in the firmament of the heavens to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years;"

Modern Corruption

Modern readings either strip 666 of its meaning (a mere spooky trope) or hunt it as an occult code—both missing that six is simply the number of man, good in labor yet fallen in pride.

expand to see more

Popular culture reduces 666 to horror-movie décor, a number to shudder at, disconnected from Revelation’s actual point—that it is “the number of a man,” humanity organized against God. The dread is superstition; the meaning is doctrine.

The occult corruption runs the other way, calculating names for the beast as though the text were a cipher to crack. Scripture gives six a plain sense—man and his labor, and man in rebellion—that needs discernment, not decoding.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Old English siex and Hebrew shesh; the theology comes from the sixth day of creation and the six days of labor, not from number-magic.

expand to see more

Old English siex — six.

Hebrew shesh — six; the day man was made and the span of his labor.

Greek hex — six; behind hexakosioi in the 666 of Revelation.

Pattern: six (man/labor) → seven (God/rest) — the creature crowned only in Sabbath.

Usage

"Six days of labor are dignified work, but they are ordered toward the seventh-day rest they cannot supply."

"The 666 is “the number of a man”—humanity in a mock trinity, ever falling short of the seven of God."

"To call six the number of man is to humble him: a worker made to rest in his Maker, not a maker who never rests."
